setup: Before this story opens, the Roman Empire had run the entire Mediterranean world for five centuries — one government, one army, one road network, one official language across three continents. By the 400s the western half is exhausted: a century of civil wars, a collapsing tax base, and wave after wave of Germanic peoples pushed across the Rhine and Danube by the Huns at their backs. Rome's own answer had been to hire those peoples as its soldiers — so by 476 the "barbarians" are not an outside horde, they are the Roman army's rank and file: Christian, Latin-speaking, led by generals who spent their careers serving Rome. What is at stake in this chapter is not a battle. It is whether "Rome" still means anything once those soldiers stop pretending there is an emperor worth obeying. The empire is not conquered. It is quietly subdivided by the men who were already running it.

bridge: Chapter 1 left the West carved into Germanic kingdoms — Visigoths in Spain, Theodoric's Ostrogoths in Italy, Vandals in Africa, and the now-Catholic Franks under Clovis's heirs in Gaul. The Roman state was gone in the West, but the Roman world was not: cities still functioned, Latin still ruled, the Church still administered, and most of these kings governed through Roman officials and styled themselves Rome's caretakers. From the surviving eastern half of the empire, ruled out of Constantinople, that did not look like a permanent settlement. It looked like territory waiting to be taken back.
setup: The man who decides to take it back is Justinian, who comes to the eastern throne in 527 with the money, the lawyers, the generals, and the conviction that there should be one Roman empire again. He has reason to think it possible: the Germanic kingdoms are divided, militarily thin, and cut off from their own Catholic subjects by the Arian heresy they follow. Three great projects define his reign — a total codification of Roman law, the most ambitious church ever built, and the military reconquest of the lost West. Two of the three succeed brilliantly. But reconquering Italy means twenty years of siege warfare that wrecks the country it was meant to save, and in 541 something nobody planned for arrives by ship from the East: the first bubonic plague pandemic in history. Whether late antiquity survives at all is what this chapter settles — and the deciding factor turns out to be a bacterium, not an army.

bridge: The political story has now run through collapse twice. Chapter 1's Germanic kings took over a still-Roman world; Chapter 2's wars and the Plague of Justinian then gutted the cities and finished off the classical urban order — Rome itself fell from roughly a million people to maybe thirty thousand. Two things were left standing in the rubble: the bishops, still holding the shrunken old Roman towns, and a brand-new institution almost nobody had noticed yet — the monastery. The major players of the last two chapters (Justinian, the Goths, the Lombards who walked into Italy in 568) were soldiers and emperors. The players of this one are monks — and they will outlast every one of those armies.
setup: Christianity is not new — the Roman Mediterranean has been officially Christian since the 300s — but in 500 it is thin, city-based, and clustered in the old Roman south, and the machinery that once spread it (imperial sponsorship, urban bishops, a working road network) is broken. So the conversion of pagan Europe is carried out, over three centuries, not by popes or armies but by monks: small bands of celibate men planting self-sufficient religious communes on the frontier and waiting for the locals to come to them. What it is replacing is not one thing but several — Germanic and Celtic paganism in the north, the rival Arian version of Christianity most of the Germanic kings adopted first, and the stubborn half-pagan folk religion of the countryside. The resistance is rarely a battlefield: it is pagan kings in Frisia and Saxony, an independent-minded Irish church that even calculates Easter its own way, and the sheer inertia of villages. Two separate engines drive the work — an Italian one founded by Benedict of Nursia, and an Irish one launched from a speck of an island off Scotland. Which of them prevails, and whether they can be reconciled at all, decides what kind of Christianity the new Europe inherits.

bridge: Three chapters in, the West has a recognizable shape: Germanic kingdoms ruling a Romanized population, a Church that survived the wreckage, and — from Chapter 3 — a monastic-and-episcopal system knitting it all into a single Latin Christendom under the bishop of Rome. The Mediterranean is poorer and more dangerous than in Roman times but still the old Roman sea, Christian on every shore. The Franks are the strongest of the kingdoms, though their Merovingian kings have dwindled to ceremonial figureheads while real power slides to their chief stewards. That is the world — settling down, Christianizing, assuming its real threats are internal — that is about to be hit from a direction nobody was watching.
setup: In 632 a new religion and a unified Arab state explode out of Arabia, and within one human lifetime they take Syria, Egypt, Persia, and the whole North African coast — every Christian shore of the southern Mediterranean, gone. In 711 an Arab-Berber army crosses into Spain and destroys the Visigothic kingdom, the most Romanized of the successor states, in seven years. The southern Mediterranean is not contested; it is lost, and lost permanently. This chapter answers two questions. First: how far does the wave reach into western Europe? Everyone remembers Charles Martel and the Battle of Tours — the real answer is more complicated and the battle far less decisive than the legend. Second, and bigger: what does the emergency do to the Franks? The steward family that supplies the man who fights at Tours uses the crisis to seize the crown outright and to seal an alliance with a pope who badly needs a protector. The partnership that will run medieval Europe for centuries is born out of this loss.

bridge: Chapter 4 ended with a coup made respectable by a pope. Pippin the Short — son of the Charles Martel who held the line at Tours — deposed the last figurehead Merovingian king in 751, had himself anointed with holy oil like an Old Testament king, and in return marched into Italy and handed the pope a kingdom of his own, the Papal States. The Frankish crown and the Roman papacy are now bolted together, each making the other legitimate. Pippin dies in 768 and, in the usual Frankish fashion, splits the realm between two sons; one of them conveniently dies three years later, leaving the whole thing to the other. That other son is the subject of this chapter.
setup: Charles — Charlemagne — rules the Franks for 43 years and spends most of them at war: 53 campaigns that swallow the Lombards, the Saxons (converted at sword-point over 32 brutal years), the Bavarians, and the Avars, until he governs nearly all of Western Christendom. On Christmas Day 800 the pope sets a crown on his head and names him Emperor of the Romans — the first Western Roman emperor in 324 years, and a direct provocation to Constantinople, which still considers the title its own. But the empire is the part that does not last; it fragments within thirty years of his death. What lasts is the thing this chapter is really about: a deliberate, empire-wide program to repair Europe's broken book-and-school infrastructure — standardize the Latin, copy and save the classical texts before they rot away, train a clergy who can actually read them. It even produces a new way of forming letters on a page that you are, in an unbroken line of descent, reading right now.

bridge: Charlemagne, from Chapter 5, briefly reassembled a Roman-shaped empire and — more durably — rebuilt the West's schools, scripts, and saved libraries, all of it resting on the Frankish-papal alliance Pippin had forged. He died in 814 and, because his other sons had died before him, the whole empire passed intact and undivided to one heir, Louis the Pious. For a single generation the great reassembled realm held together under one earnest, deeply religious emperor. The catch is that holding together was a fluke of mortality, not a system — and Louis has more than one son.
setup: Frankish custom has one iron rule that no amount of imperial grandeur overrides: a king's lands are divided among his sons, like a farm. Louis the Pious tries to legislate his way around it to keep the empire whole — and then a fourth son is born and detonates the plan. Three civil wars follow, fought by brothers and their grown sons, with the Frankish nobility switching sides for twenty years. It ends in 843 at Verdun with the empire cut in three: a west that will become France, an east that will become Germany, and a doomed strip down the middle the two will fight over for the next eleven centuries. While the dynasts tear at each other, something quieter and more permanent happens beneath them: the counts and bishops who were supposed to be royal officials begin treating their offices — and the public power that comes with them — as private family property. What is at stake here is not just a map. It is whether central authority survives in Europe at all.

bridge: Chapter 6 left the central authority of the West in pieces — Charlemagne's empire split three ways at Verdun in 843 and then crumbling further, public power leaking out of royal hands into local counts and bishops who were quietly going private. The Frankish state can no longer reliably raise an army, defend a coastline, or make a royal decree stick past the next river. Into a Europe that has just lost the ability to coordinate a defense come, almost at the same moment, three different sets of enemies who could not have timed it better.
setup: From the North Sea come the Vikings — Scandinavian raiders in shallow-draft longships who can row up any river, sack a monastery, and be gone before a land army hears about it; within decades they stop raiding and start conquering and settling. From the Hungarian plain come the Magyars, steppe horse-archers who cover fifty miles a day and outrun every Western army sent against them. From Muslim Sicily and Spain come the Saracens, pirate fleets who sack Rome's own basilicas and make the western sea unsafe for two centuries. Three enemies, three directions, one broken state that can stop none of them. But the interesting part is not the raids — it is the response. With no king able to protect them, the men who can afford a horse, armor, and a fortified mound start doing it themselves, and swearing service to whoever is stronger in exchange for land to pay for it. That improvised bargain, repeated ten thousand times, is the castle, the knight, and the thing later centuries will call feudalism. The European order for the next four hundred years is being invented here, under duress.

bridge: Across the last two chapters the West fragmented at Verdun (843) and was then hammered for a century and a half by Vikings, Magyars, and Saracens, surviving only by improvising the castle, the mounted knight, and the proto-feudal bargain that scattered public power into private hands. The Carolingian dynasty guttered out kingdom by kingdom. Of the three pieces of Charlemagne's empire, the eastern one — the future Germany — came out of the triple shock in the worst shape of all: no royal authority, the Magyars raiding every year, the last Carolingian king there dead at eight years old. This final chapter is how the worst-off fragment becomes the engine of the recovery.
setup: When the eastern Frankish royal line dies out, the German dukes do something new: they elect a king from among themselves. The Saxon dukes who win that election — Henry the Fowler, then his son Otto the Great — spend four generations rebuilding. They smash the Magyars for good with heavy cavalry at Lechfeld in 955, ending the raids that had terrorized Europe for sixty years. Otto revives the Roman imperial title in 962, founding the Holy Roman Empire that will last until 1806. Underneath the politics, three slower revolutions converge: a reformed monasticism radiating out of the abbey of Cluny, the conversion of Poland, Hungary, Scandinavia, and Rus' that doubles the size of Christendom in fifty years, and a quiet agricultural revolution — a heavier plow, the horse collar, crop rotation — that finally lets northern Europe feed a growing population. By the year 1000 the long emergency is over and every ingredient of the High Middle Ages — towns, cathedrals, universities, crusades — is on the table. This chapter is the West climbing back out.
